builder_plan.scenario: Start with one repeated product task that has a measurable failure or cost.
builder_plan.change: Read the methods and identify one change you can isolate in that workflow.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current implementation on the same held-out tasks.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Successful outcomes, response time, human rework, and total cost per successful task.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: One Policy for 100 Household Tasks: Our Solution for the 2026 BEHAVIOR Challenge
summary: The method replaces per-task policies and short training runs with one vision-language-action checkpoint trained for 200k steps over 211M demonstration frames, using variance-reduced multi-sample flow matching and stage/task embeddings warm-started across tasks, plus optional routing of hard tasks to a proprietary LLM agent with motion tools. It costs a 200k-step training run on a 100-task demonstration dataset, a custom six-simulator-per-GPU evaluation infrastructure with provenance tracking, and dependence on a closed third-party model (GPT-6 Astra) for a third of the reported gains. It can fail because the learned policy alone succeeds on only a fraction of tasks (0.108 Q on the agent-routed subset), results depend on challenge-specific teleoperation data and simulator tuning that do not transfer to other domains, and the agent-routed component is not reproducible without comparable proprietary model access.
rationale: The gains rest on large-scale demonstration data, prolonged VLA training, and closed frontier-model access that exceed the reader's constrained infrastructure, making this relevant to monitor but not adoptable in production practice.
technique: Single VLA policy for multi-task household robotics

It costs a 200k-step training run on a 100-task demonstration dataset, a custom six-simulator-per-GPU evaluation infrastructure with provenance tracking, and dependence on a closed third-party model (GPT-6 Astra) for a third of the reported gains. It can fail because the learned policy alone succeeds on only a fraction of tasks (0.108 Q on the agent-routed subset), results depend on challenge-specific teleoperation data and simulator tuning that do not transfer to other domains, and the agent-routed component is not reproducible without comparable proprietary model access.
Q score rose from 0.260 to 0.371 on the 50 shared 2025 tasks (0.392 across all 100 tasks); a routed GPT-based coding agent scored 0.639 mean Q on 14 tasks versus 0.108 for the learned policy.
